newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS - up 1/4, follow Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS - up 1/4, follow Treasuries.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond prices gained around 1/4 in late trade on Thursday, aided by a stronger U.S. Treasury market.
But the lack of retail interest in munis still was seen as crimping activity.
While the market is driven by new issues, most of the business that is getting done is through bond swaps, traders said.
"I don't see a ton of things going away," one added.

Some new issues, which typically sell well with individual investors, like Westchester County, N.Y.'s $60 million of general obligation bonds and Millburn, N.J.'s $4.85 million of general improvement bonds, were considered fairly costly.
For example, one trader said his firm did not participate in either offering because they were priced too aggressively, though he noted both localities carry high ratings.
Westchester sold its bonds at a 4.68 percent net interest cost. The Millburn debt was sold with a rate of 4.60 percent.
A similar pattern was seen with Virgina's sale of $184 million of transport bonds, which were awarded to Lehman at a true interest cost of 5.34 percent, a level also considered fairly aggressive.
But traders said that there appeared to be strong interest in the state's term bonds, from around 2021-25. "It seems like that's getting cleaned up," one said.
Another major sale was Chicago's sale of $183 million of Skyway revenue bonds, which were repriced with some lower yields, although the top yield in 2023 was unchanged at about 5.799 percent.

In the secondary market, Metropolitan Pier & Exposition Authority Illinois Dedicated State Tax Revenue Refunding of June 2027, which carry a 5-1/4 percent coupon, were bid at 5.68 percent, down three basis points.
And Delaware River Port Authority of Pennsylvania & New Jersey revenue bonds of January 2026, which have a 5-1/2 percent coupon, were bid at 5.63 percent, down two basis points.

Despite the strong demand for new issues, traders were wary of the effect that the strong equities markets have had in siphoning off individual investors, who otherwise might have bought municipal bonds.
"As long as the stock market looks like it's going to produce a 10 percent return, why invest in municipals at five percent?" a trader said, explaining the reasoning of the retail crowd.
This could bode ill for the start of the year, when the municipal market typically gets a boost from new money that is invested.
"Generally, you get a big run-up in January, when a lot of new money comes in the market. We'll have to see if we capture that money or if it goes elsewhere," a trader said.

On the Chicago Board of Trade, December municipal bond futures rose 18 ticks to 117-13/32. December Treasury futures achieved the same 18-tick gain, climing to 115-9/32. The MOB spread stood at 68 ticks.
